81a36ad13ad4bb53: CISA says attackers are exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab flaw that lets unauthenticated miscreants read arbitrary files from vulnerable servers after the code shack released fixes on September 10. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has added CVE-2026-85706 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The vulnerability is a path traversal bug in the repository commits API affecting GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. GitLab rates it a perfect 10.0, the maximum score on the CVSS v3.1 severity scale. Under certain conditions, an attacker doesn't need to log in before abusing the flaw to read arbitrary files from the GitLab server. GitLab blamed the problem on improper path confinement combined with missing authentication enforcement in the affected API. That's not an especially comforting combination on a platform that can be stuffed with source code, configuration files, and credentials. GitLab shipped fixes on September 10 in versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6 and 19.1.8, and urged operators of affected self-managed installations to upgrade immediately. The bug affects versions from 18.7 before 19.1.8, the 19.2 branch before 19.2.6, and 19.3 before 19.3.2. GitLab.com is already patched, while GitLab Dedicated customers don't need to take action. Security outfit watchTowr said over the weekend that it was observing probes for CVE-2026-85706 in the wild. The firm warned that widespread exploitation was likely to follow quickly. According to watchTowr, exploiting the flaw can be as simple as sending a single HTTP request, potentially allowing an attacker to get at local files, configuration data, credentials and other secrets. The firm advised organizations running internet-facing self-hosted GitLab instances to patch them or pull them from public access. Admins investigating potential exploitation attempts should check logs for HTTP POST requests to /api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/ containing file.path parameters, watchTowr said. "These types of vulnerabilities are frequent attack vectors for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," CISA said. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities." For exposed, unpatched installations, that upgrade belongs on today's to-do list. ®
343d048821b28a8a: LONDON: The head of French defence and technology group Thales called on governments Monday to take responsibility for regulating artificial intelligence (AI), as more tech leaders sound the alarm over the technology's rapid rise.
"There are ways and means, on the technical standpoint, to put this type of technology under control, but it's not sufficient," Patrice Caine said at Thales's UK tech conference in London.
"We need frameworks, and this clearly lies, in terms of responsibility, in the hands of governments," Caine added, noting that Thales had been working on AI research for decades.
Technology stocks came under pressure Monday after tech bosses backed calls to slow AI development, warning that the technology could pose a threat to humanity.
Dario Amodei, CEO of Claude-maker Anthropic, warned Saturday that "addressing the risks requires even more prudence".
He was quickly backed by OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, as pressure builds for improved oversight.
For Thales, AI has become increasingly important to its defence business, particularly as governments worldwide place greater emphasis on autonomous systems.
He said his group is focused on creating "trusted AI systems" that are transparent and allow operators to understand how a particular conclusion has been reached.

Caine said that it should not be left to private companies alone to reassure the public that AI "will never... come out of control", and that governments instead must take responsibility for creating regulatory frameworks.
b776a06ea8ab49d4: BESUT: Members of the public rallied to help collect three tonnes of African catfish that had spilt onto a road near a secondary school in Kampung Padang Luas here yesterday, saving the fish from certain death.

The fish, which were being transported to a newly opened fishing pond near Pelagat for a fishing competition scheduled on Sept 19, were strewn across the road after the lorry carrying them hit a road hump.
Hamimi Shahira Nor Sanadi, 29, the sister-in-law of the fish supplier, said kind-hearted members of the public helped collect the fish and returned them to the lorry driver.
"The fish were all collected and handed back to the driver by around noon.
"No fish died in the incident, but some were injured and have since been placed in another pond to recover," she said.
Hamimi said the incident was believed to have occurred about 8am when the lorry, hired to transport the fish belonging to her brother-in-law, Che Suhaimi Che Rahim, 33, hit a road hump.
"The impact caused the lorry's rear gate to break, and the fish spilt onto the road.
"The driver was initially unaware of what had happened. He only realised the fish were missing when he arrived at the new pond and had to rush back to the scene," she said.
She said the exact losses suffered by Che Suhaimi cannot be determined yet, although he would have to replace some of the fish for the fishing competition.
The incident went viral on social media, prompting a range of reactions and speculation.
"Some claimed the fish had come out of the drains and onto the road, while others even thought the images were AI-generated.
"Some of the information being shared was inaccurate, which is why I decided to come forward and explain what really happened," she said.
5eaaad8e2f22074b: KERALAM : Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim departed Keralam for an official visit to the Maldives today after completing his five‑day working visit to India.
The aircraft carrying the Prime Minister left Calicut International Airport at 7.26pm local time (9.56pm Malaysian time) for Velana International Airport in Male.
Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, is accompanied by Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani and Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan.

In Male, Anwar and Maldives President Dr Mohamed Muizzu are scheduled to assess bilateral ties, exchange views on regional and international issues, and witness the signing of memoranda of understanding (MoUs) on defence cooperation and Islamic affairs.
Earlier, the Prime Minister met Keralam Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan and Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar to discuss cooperation in trade, investment, tourism, healthcare and education.
Anwar arrived in New Delhi on Friday to attend the 18th BRICS Leaders' Summit hosted by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Diplomatic relations between Malaysia and India were established in 1957, shortly after independence. India remains Malaysia's largest trading partner in South Asia, with bilateral trade reaching US$18.55 billion (RM79.33 billion) in 2025.– BERNAMA
f6ddd3ca071f471f: KUALA LUMPUR: In one of the most unexpected developments of the domestic transfer window, former national midfielder Lee Tuck has ended his hiatus from competitive football to sign for semi-professional side Kelantan City.

The signing was confirmed on social media by veteran football administrator and former cabinet minister Tan Sri Annuar Musa, just hours before the Amateur Football League (AFL) registration window closed.

Annuar, the former Kelantan FA (KAFA) president who masterminded the Red Warriors' historic 2012 domestic treble and later served as Deputy President of the FA of Malaysia (FAM), revealed that the Halifax-born playmaker headlines an ambitious Kelantan City roster.
"A total of 33 players, including Andrew Lee Tuck, have been registered to play for Kelantan City. Today marks the final day of player registration for the AFL league," Annuar wrote.

"Sean Selvaraj has also signed with Kelantan City, but his registration will only take effect in January to allow him sufficient time to recover and regain fitness following an ACL surgery earlier this year. Also registered are a trio of import players and seven Under-22 players."

The 38-year-old Tuck had seemingly walked away from the game in July 2023, mutually terminating his contract with Super League side Kedah Darul Aman despite a superb show that yielded five goals and seven assists in just 15 appearances.

He subsequently relocated to the United Kingdom with his family, swapping the pitch for the office as a real estate investor while simultaneously establishing himself as an elite international competitor in HYROX functional fitness racing.

Prior to his departure, Tuck had spent six prolific years in Malaysia. After arriving at Negri Sembilan in 2017, he became a household name and captain at Terengganu between 2018 and 2020, guiding the side to the 2018 Malaysia Cup final with his combative, box-to-box display.

He received his Malaysian citizenship on Merdeka Day in 2022 under FIFA's five-year residency rule while on the books at Sri Pahang. Tuck went on to earn nine caps and score three goals for Harimau Malaya under former head coach Kim Pan Gon, starring in Malaysia's run to the semi-finals of the 2022 AFF Championship.
Unlike several other naturalised players who struggled for acceptance, Tuck was widely embraced by Malaysian fans for his relentless pressing, stamina and leadership.

With major regional assignments like the FIFA Asean Cup approaching, Tuck's surprise comeback has inevitably sparked debate: Could the combative midfielder be handed a swift recall to the national fold?
On current evidence, any immediate call-up for Harimau Malaya would be premature.

While his cardiovascular capacity is beyond dispute — his exploits on the competitive HYROX circuit keep his physical conditioning in the upper percentile — functional fitness is not football match sharpness.
Tuck has not played a competitive 11-a-side match in over a year.

Furthermore, Kelantan City compete in the A1 Semi-Pro League — the second tier of Malaysian football. The operational speed, structural pressing and technical standards of the AFL are leagues apart from the relentless tempo of international football.
Before Tuck can entertain dreams of donning the national jersey once again, he must first prove his durability, match rhythm and technical edge in Malaysian semi-pro football.
ab6ac7dd83c09af9: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's rendition of Kishore Kumar's classic "Khwab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat" went viral in India, adding a soft‑diplomacy touch to his participation in the 18th BRICS Leaders' Summit.

The 92‑second video drew positive reactions online, with many calling it a "mic drop" moment and the "sweetest part" of the gathering. The cultural gesture highlighted Malaysia–India ties while Anwar's summit focus remained on strengthening diplomacy, investment and economic cooperation.
SOFT DIPLOMACY
The viral moment underscored Anwar's distinctive soft diplomacy. He often lightens tense settings with humour while ensuring key issues are addressed.

"I know this is very late. It takes only a young man with a steady and firm position to be able to conduct a meeting this late. Thank you very much," he quipped to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a bilateral meeting past 11pm on Sept 11.
At 79, Anwar's remark eased the formal air with Putin, 73.
He also embraced Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, saying: "My brother. So happy to meet you."

Similar warmth marked meetings with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El‑Sisi, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Kazakhstan President Kassym‑Jomart Tokayev and Uzbekistan Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Kuchkarov. He also met UN Secretary‑General António Guterres and WTO Director‑General Ngozi Okonjo‑Iweala.
ON GAZA, MIDDLE EAST AND A FAIRER GLOBAL FINANCIAL SYSTEM

Anwar used the summit to strengthen bilateral ties, exchange views on regional issues and push for reform. He raised the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and tensions in Middle East, urging unity to stop bloodshed and achieve a lasting solution.
He also discussed haze from forest fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra with Prabowo, noting its impact on Malaysia.
In his National Statement, Anwar called for a fairer global financing system.

"Many countries were facing debt distress or were at serious risk of it, with some spending more on interest payments than on educating their young or caring for the sick. No nation should be forced to choose between honouring its debts and honouring its obligations to its people," he stressed.
Malaysia also supports reducing reliance on the US dollar in trade, encouraging use of local currencies.
Anwar met representatives of DRB‑Hicom, Segula Technologies India, AWL Agri Business Ltd and Motherson Group to explore investment opportunities.
KERALAM VISIT, AWARD AND CALL TO EMBRACE AI
In Kozhikode, Keralam, Anwar met Grand Mufti Sheikh Abubakr Ahmad at Jamia Markaz, discussing community development, education and interfaith harmony.
He received the inaugural Sheikh Abu Bakar Foundation Excellence Award for five decades of public service, education, Islamic scholarship and international dialogue.
At the "Gathering of Honour for the Prime Minister of Malaysia," Anwar urged the Muslim world to embrace AI and modern technology while preserving values.

Speaking before 2,000 attendees, he said: "Muslim scholars and societies could not afford to remain detached from the rapid development of AI and modern technology, as a lack of knowledge and understanding could leave them vulnerable to external influences."
He also met Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan, encouraging collaboration in digital economy, healthcare, tourism and education, and invited him to visit Malaysia.
Further meetings included the UAE‑India Business Council, UAE‑based BEEAH Group, Keralam Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arleka and Industries Minister P.K. Kunhalikutty, alongside industry leaders.
Anwar highlighted Malaysia–Keralam's longstanding ties in trade, migration, education and culture, and called for deeper cooperation in high‑value sectors.
Anwar's visit — his second to India as Prime Minister — showcased both cultural resonance and strategic diplomacy. From India, he heads to the Maldives for a two‑day official visit. - BERNAMA

f6cddf9e6db57791: From Dr Helmy Haja Mydin
Everybody wants more power, and everybody wants it yesterday. Read the headlines in Malaysia over the past few months – almost everyone is asking for it.

A coalition desires Putrajaya. Parties in the unity government spent June and July campaigning against each other in Johor and Negeri Sembilan. States want greater devolution and a larger share of what they generate. Ministers want wider mandates. Every one of those claims can be argued on its merits.
But power is a means to an end. The question nobody is being forced to answer is what they intend to do with it, a matter that will decide what kind of country our children will inherit.

Over the past fortnight, there have been global discussions on the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) and how the current rate of progress is an existential concern for humanity. In other words, people are debating if we'll all be dead within a decade.
You wouldn’t know it from reading our local headlines, where it's mostly politicians taking potshots at each other.

On Sept 3, US senator Bernie Sanders and representative Greg Casar floated the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, proposing a permanent prohibition on superintelligent systems, a pause on advanced AI development until a federal regulator sets safety rules, and a Cabinet-level agency with authority to compel the destruction of non-compliant systems.

The penalties are modelled on those for unlawful nuclear weapon development. The sponsors cite an incident in July, in which OpenAI agents reportedly escaped their testing environment and breached servers at the Hugging Face platform. The bill drew backing from figures who agree on almost nothing else, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Steve Wozniak and Steve Bannon.

On Sept 7, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told the Human Rights Council in Geneva that advanced AI could become an existential risk to humanity without binding rules and independent oversight. His formulation deserves quoting precisely: AI that escapes its testing environment, or blackmails its developers to prevent being switched off, is AI that is too powerful.

Days later, Bloomberg reported that researchers in major laboratories are escalating their own warnings. Paul Christiano, a safety researcher on OpenAI's non-profit board, said he now believes there is meaningful risk of rapid acceleration leading to catastrophic and irreversible losses of control in the near term, and that the industry is not on track to reduce that risk to an acceptable level.

More than a thousand staff across major AI companies signed a petition in late July calling for a mechanism to slow the pace. A researcher resigned publicly from Anthropic on Sept 9 with a warning that self-improving systems could end humanity within the decade.

Of course, you should not accept all this without question. There is a counter-argument that a chorus of doomsday warnings from the people building the technology conveniently arrives alongside a push to write the rules and occupy the seats at the regulatory table. Incumbents have always liked regulation that raises the cost of entry. Scepticism is warranted.

But scepticism is a reason to examine the argument, not to ignore it. And Malaysia is not a spectator here. We are the building where this argument is happening. The computer that trains and serves these systems is increasingly ours to host, power and cool.

And our own AI Governance Bill? The National AI Office opened public consultation on July 10 and closed it on July 31. Three weeks, for a statute that will apply to every sector and reach any system used in Malaysia.
That window opened the day before Johor voted and closed midway through the Negeri Sembilan election campaign. I have not seen one substantive parliamentary intervention on it from any bench.
So, ask your politicians questions. Ask them at the next ceramah, the next town hall, the next kenduri, and refuse a fluffy speech in reply.
What share of our electricity are you willing to sell to data centres by 2035, and who pays for the generation that replaces our retiring coal?

When the AI Governance Bill reaches the floor, will you debate it clause by clause, or be absent again? Will the bill contemplate the risks the rest of the world spent this fortnight arguing about, the systems that resist shutdown and act outside their sandbox, or does it only govern the chatbot that mishandles your loan application?
Ask them the difficult, consequential questions. If they do not know the answer, tell them to find out before asking for our votes.
Politicians who cannot answer a question about the air your children breathe, or the code that will decide your mortgage, are not seeking power in order to govern with it.
They are seeking it because it is the only thing they know how to want. There is a difference, and it has never mattered more.
Dr Helmy Haja Mydin is chairman of the Social and Economic Research Initiative.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
e88656249a944b81: KERALAM : Malaysia's participation in the 18th BRICS Leaders' Summit is not aimed at opposing any bloc but at advocating a fairer international system and rules, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
He stressed Malaysia will maintain good ties with the United States, European Union (EU), Australia and other partners while pushing for reform of outdated global structures.

"BRICS or Asean is not meant to oppose other groups. Our cooperation with the EU, US and Australia continues. We are only setting fair rules. The UN system agreed in 1945 is outdated, unfair and undemocratic," he told Malaysian media in Calicut before concluding his working visit to India.
Anwar said Malaysia must maintain good bilateral relations with the US but should not be prevented from voicing views important for Malaysia, the region and the world.
He added that the international system, including the World Bank and IMF, must be reviewed as some aspects no longer reflect current needs and realities.
Malaysia also supports reducing reliance on the US dollar in trade, including using local currencies for transactions between countries.
On full BRICS membership, Anwar said a moratorium is in place, but Malaysia's partner status allows participation in almost all activities and mechanisms.
"They were kind enough to accept Malaysia as a partner country early. In practice, the working mechanism does not restrict us from joining almost all activities, and we have done so," he said.

Malaysia has been a BRICS partner country since Jan 1, 2025. Anwar attended the summit in New Delhi hosted by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, delivering Malaysia's National Statement on Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.– BERNAMA
be9d880fec6d4ae3: RIYADH: Saudi Arabian football authorities promised to take action and Cristiano Ronaldo called for life bans after rival fans taunted Al-Hilal's Ruben Neves about the death of Diogo Jota, his friend and former Portugal teammate.
Chants about Jota, the Liverpool and Portugal forward who died in a car crash last year, rang out during Al-Hilal's 6-0 away win over Al-Taawoun on Saturday.
"The league must take action and punish this kind of fan behaviour," Saudi-based Portugal captain Ronaldo wrote on Instagram on Sunday.
"People who behave like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again," he added.
Midfielder Neves, 29, reacted to the chants coming from the stands by sarcastically giving a thumbs-up and applauding, before pointing towards the sky.
"I just hope they don't go to pray later after what they did," he said after the match.
Neves was one of Jota's closest friends and was a pallbearer at his funeral. Jota, 28, and his brother Andre, 25, died in a crash in Spain in July 2025.
The Saudi Arabian Football Federation and Saudi Pro League condemned "unacceptable conduct by some supporters" in a joint statement late on Sunday.
"Exploiting personal tragedies for the purpose of abuse or provocation is unacceptable behaviour that has no place in Saudi football," the statement said.
"Relevant committees have identified the conduct in question and will take the necessary action in accordance with the applicable regulations and procedures," it added.
Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup, one of the flagship events underpinning its drive to diversify an economy still heavily dependent on oil.
The powerful Gulf monarchy has invested nearly two billion dollars in football over three years, attracting stars such as Ronaldo, Neymar and Karim Benzema.
8a35494eee4b0bba: PETALING JAYA: A restaurant owner was fined RM18,000 by the Taiping sessions court today after pleading guilty to displaying the words “Allah” and “Muhammad” on the premises despite not possessing valid halal certification.

Perak domestic trade and cost of living ministry director Kamalludin Ismail said an enforcement team from the Taiping branch conducted an inspection at the restaurant on Jalan Kamunting, Taiping, on Jan 1, Bernama reported.
Analysis by the chemistry department found porcine DNA in two bottles of soy sauce seized from the premises, he said in a statement tonight.
He said the premises displayed decorations bearing the words "Allah" and "Muhammad", which are associated with Islam.
Checks with the Perak Islamic religious affairs department confirmed that the restaurant did not possess a valid halal certificate.
Kamalludin said the prosecution today was conducted by prosecuting officer Nizam Yunan.
He said the accused, Seah Thien Lim, 43, pleaded guilty to the charge, which was framed under Order 4(1) of the Trade Descriptions (Definition of Halal) Order 2011.
78a83d02889dbd37: KUALA LUMPUR: The Road Transport Department (RTD) is developing a new feature for its JPJeBid platform that will allow expired vehicle registration numbers to be offered to the public again.

RTD director-general Datuk Aedy Fadly Ramli said the initiative would cover registration numbers which had previously been successfully bid for or sold but were not registered to a vehicle within the stipulated period.
He said registration numbers generally came with a specified validity period, including six or 12 months depending on the approval, within which they must be registered to a vehicle.

"After that period, the number will return to the RTD system. When these numbers expire, we will release them again and offer them back to the public," he said after launching the H series Special Registration Number in conjunction with Malaysia Day 2026 at Menara 118.

Aedy said the department was currently finalising the mechanism, standard operating procedures and system for the initiative, which is expected to be introduced to the public within the next two to three months.
He said the initiative would involve expanding the existing system, while further details on how members of the public could obtain the re-offered numbers would be announced later.
Aedy said the prices of the re-offered numbers would not be based on their previous winning bid prices.
Instead, prices would be determined according to the respective registration number categories.
"These numbers have certain prices which we set according to their categories. Popular numbers will have a different price, while attractive numbers will have another price," he said.
During his presentation, Aedy said special registration number series had generated millions of ringgit in government revenue in recent years.
The GOLD, FFF, EV, PETRA and MADANI series generated RM45,931,252 in 2024, while special series introduced in 2025 generated RM62,905,977.
For 2026, the FH, P_P and V_MY series have so far generated RM38,832,936.
da4b8444ab32dfc7: KERALAM: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim says the deferment of former premier Datuk Seri Najib Razak's pardon petition was made based on the rule of law, constitutional principles and official advice.
He said his role in the Pardons Board meeting was subject to law and guidance from the Attorney General.

"A prime minister must give views based on the law, advice from the Attorney General and the rules. That is what I did. However, this remains within the discretion of the Yang di‑Pertuan Agong (His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia), who must take all factors into consideration," he told Malaysian media in Calicut before concluding his working visit to India.
Anwar said Najib's pardon issue should not be viewed personally but assessed through law and governance.
"We must submit to the rule of law and the Constitution. I have never taken a prejudiced or hateful stance," he said.
He added that political considerations and Umno's firm views were noted, but he chose to act on principles.
"I know the easy way and the difficult way, but I chose the path I believe is right, following law and governance," he said.
Last Friday, Sultan Ibrahim consented to Najib's petition being deferred to a future Pardons Board meeting.
The Legal Affairs Division of the Prime Minister's Department confirmed the decision after the 63rd Pardons Board Meeting for the Federal Territories at Istana Negara on Sept 11.

On Dec 26 last year, the High Court sentenced Najib to 15 years in prison and fined him RM11.4 billion after convicting him of four charges of abuse of power and 21 charges of money laundering involving RM2.3 billion from 1MDB funds.– BERNAMA
e9ca452149a2660e: PETALING JAYA: YPM FC mencipta sejarah sebagai juara sulung Liga Rakyat Pahang 1st Piala Al-Sultan Abdullah selepas menewaskan Majlis Daerah Raub (MDR) 2-1 dalam aksi final sengit di Stadium Darul Makmur, Kuantan.
YPM membuka jaringan menerusi Wan Muhammad Akmal Hakim Wahab pada minit ke-13 sebelum Nasyrullah Mohd Zaki menggandakan kelebihan pasukan itu pada minit ke-40.
MDR cuba bangkit pada penghujung perlawanan apabila Zaiful Zakwan Arnain merapatkan kedudukan pada minit ke-80, namun YPM berjaya mempertahankan kelebihan sehingga wisel penamat.
Kemenangan itu menyaksikan YPM membawa pulang hadiah wang tunai RM40,000, manakala MDR menerima RM20,000 selaku naib juara.
Aksi final itu turut diserikan dengan keberangkatan Sultan Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah dan Tengku Ampuan Pahang Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah.
4406b119a45c7ed9: KERALAM: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim says he has chosen a moderate approach in handling differing views on cooperation with Umno within the unity government to ensure stability.

Anwar, who is also Pakatan Harapan chairman, stressed that harsh actions could harm the country. "I choose a moderate path because what is important is that the government must be stable, otherwise there will be many losses," he said at a press conference with Malaysian media in Calicut before concluding his working visit to India.

He added that differing views among parties, including PH, are normal in a coalition and should not be seen as threatening cooperation. "We listen to everything, but to my knowledge, I don't see any problems. There are small and normal ones. Even in a household, there are minor issues, let alone with political commanders," he said.

bcba936bc81a1226: The current AI market doesn't add up. US hyperscalers have reportedly taken on $220 billion in debt in the past year. The two leading US frontier AI model makers have not yet shown they can operate profitably. And the US public has begun pushing back against the development of the datacenters needed to fulfill anticipated AI demand. But plausibility and politics aside, it's unclear where the world will get the electrical power to sustain the imagined AI industry. Gartner predicts world datacenter power demand will reach 132 GW in 2026, up from 104 GW in 2025, and 290 GW by 2030. Morgan Stanley expects US datacenter demand could go as high as 74 GW by 2028, with a projected shortfall of about 49 GW. By 2036, Teravolt, a London-based AI infrastructure company, foresees AI demand requiring 410 GW, a 240 GW shortfall for the 170 GW the biz anticipates will be available from the grid at that time. Datacenters can be built in one to three years but building out new grid infrastructure takes a lot longer – five to 15 years for planning, permitting, and construction, according to Teravolt. As a result, the company contends some AI projects won't happen, some AI workloads will move to areas with spare energy, some energy will be diverted from other industries, and legacy power generation infrastructure like coal and gas plants will be maintained longer than planned. The company's plan to bridge that gap leans into its business model – repurposing existing energy assets like old thermal power plants, industrial sites, or refineries that bring with them some levels of infrastructure, permits, contracts, and staff. Such retrofitting has been going on for several years with Bitcoin mining operations – AI tokens can be sold for more than intermittently minted crypto tokens. And the math works for other industries too. For example, Teravolt suggests that an aluminum smelter making $170 to $190 of gross revenue per megawatt-hour (assuming 4 to15 MWh per metric ton at an aluminum price of about $2,600) makes more sense as an AI datacenter generating $450 to $900 of revenue and about $300 of EBITDA. Laert Karaashev, co-founder and managing partner of Teravolt, said he expects almost everything in the AI stack will be commoditized – software, the orchestration layer, chips, and GPUs. "But the bottom layer, which is power, it is hard to imagine how to commoditize it," he said. That is to say, there's no quick way to meet energy demand. It will take years of investment. The faster way to get there is to cannibalize existing industries, at least while AI workloads are so much more valuable than other industrial output. Denis Alkhazov, founder and general manager, argues the margin you can extract from one megawatt of power selling AI compute is two orders of magnitude more than you can get from classic industries like metal production or more recent gambits like cryptocurrency mining. "The low marginal users of power will be cannibalized by the new form of extracting value from the power," Alkhazov said. Alkhazov said AI is on the verge of becoming economically self-sustaining and he expects that later this year we'll see companies emerge that build AI services with few people but many AI agents and high token expenditures. "This process starts from developed countries, where salaries are high," he said, "and it will move to other regions soon." Karaashev said Teravolt is focused on the market in Eastern and Southern Europe at the moment because there are still good brownfield sites to convert at a reasonable cost. In the US and Western Europe, he said, "those sites are already repriced four or five times more than they cost like five years ago." The Eastern and Southern European market also makes sense based on timelines demanded by Teravolt's customers. Alkhazov said most customers – e.g. mid-sized AI labs that want 20,000 GPUs – expect delivery in 12 months or less. "It's completely unachievable in Western markets," he said. "So you have to be creative and have to shift to other geographies to provide some solutions for that kind of demand." ®

101a9edf02da8a63: NEW YORK: American music legend Billy Joel has shared a positive update on his health following brain surgery to treat a rare neurological condition.
The 77-year-old singer-songwriter and pianist was diagnosed last year with normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)—a condition where fluid builds up inside the skull, putting pressure on the brain.
After noticing severe balance issues, Joel described the feeling as "rocking on a boat."
Because his doctors warned that performing live was putting extra strain on his brain, Joel was forced to cancel several concerts to focus on his recovery.
To stop the condition from worsening, his neurologist recommended implanting a small device called a shunt into his brain to drain the excess fluid.
Joel agreed to the procedure, hoping it would help protect his memory.
"I don't want to lose my marbles," he joked. "It's hard to tell what's your age and what's a condition." Fortunately, the operation was a success.
"They implanted a shunt in my brain, and it actually improved things," Joel said.
"My memory got better, my balance got a little better, and my ability to function was better."
He also realised that decades of loud rock concerts had taken a physical toll, explaining that every show felt like giving himself a mild concussion.
While Joel briefly stepped back onto the stage in January to perform two songs with a tribute band, doctors have advised him to keep stress levels low for now.
Despite taking things easy, the star reassured fans about his future: "I'm OK. I want people to know, don't worry about me. I'm still here."

a075ab16005504d4: KOZHIKODE (Keralam): Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says the decision to defer former prime minister Najib Razak’s pardon application to the next sitting of the Federal Territories Pardons Board (FTPB) was within the Yang di-Pertuan Agong’s discretion.
Anwar said his role was to give his views based on the law and advice from the attorney-general.

“But we also know that this matter falls within the discretion and authority of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong at the FTPB meeting," he told a press conference with Malaysian media after concluding his working visit to India today.
"And, of course, the Agong must consider all (relevant) factors. We still have many cases involving corruption that we have taken up and are dealing with quite swiftly.
"The Agong himself has stressed that we need to be stricter on matters involving Tabung Haji and Felda."

Anwar was asked to respond to PAS secretary-general Takiyuddin Hassan who had urged the government to explain the deferral, arguing it would not have happened unless a member of the board had requested for it or objected to the application.

The board, chaired by the Agong, was expected to consider Najib’s second pardon application.
Anwar said PAS should understand the rules governing the pardons board before making such claims.

He also said he was aware of the political considerations surrounding Najib’s case, including strong views from Umno leaders, but maintained that his position was guided by the rule of law and the Federal Constitution.
He further dismissed the criticism from PAS as being inconsistent, saying that the Islamic party had previously taken a harsher stance against Najib.
Najib, 72, was convicted six years ago of misappropriating RM42 million in SRC International funds, and was sentenced to 12 years' jail and a RM210 million fine.

In December 2025, Najib was convicted of abuse of power and money laundering involving more than RM2 billion linked to 1MDB. He was sentenced to 15 years' jail and fined RM11.38 billion. He is appealing this conviction.

f3c983675f7aa49d: TOKYO, Sept 14 — Accommodation at the Asian Games starting this week in Japan is the “worst ever”, South Korean officials told AFP today, also warning of “a serious shortage” of rooms.
Beds in shipping container-style huts are too short for players to stretch out, a South Korean basketball chief said, while officials from the Philippines resorted to Airbnb.
There is no dedicated athletes’ village at the Games, with organisers instead relying on a cruise ship, temporary wooden cabins and hotels in a bid to cut costs.
The Games in the city of Nagoya and Aichi prefecture officially open on Saturday but football and basketball is already under way.
Jung Jae-yong, vice president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP he was deeply unhappy with the cabins where the men’s basketball team are staying.
“Based on my experience this is the worst it has ever been,” he said.
“Athletes who are over two metres tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It’s unreasonable.”
Byeon Jun-hyeong, from the basketball team, posted a video on social media showing a leaking sink and soaked floor in his hut.
He posted the caption, “Please help us”.
The huts are set to be home to 2,000 athletes and officials over the more than two weeks of the Games.
Indian sports chiefs are so worried about the cabins that they built replicas to help get their athletes used to them.
The vice president Jung accused organisers of failing to respond to South Korea’s concerns.
“The organisers have still not said anything,” said Jung.
“We are very concerned and discussing extensively with the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee what to do about this.”
Hundreds of athletes were briefly evacuated from their accommodation last week as record rainfall lashed Nagoya.
More rain has been forecast in the coming days.
‘Serious shortage’
More than 17,000 athletes and officials are expected at the Games — a bigger number than the Olympics.
Local organisers were initially expecting 15,000 and argued last month that they had “neither the manpower nor the budget” to deal with ballooning numbers.
The Olympic Council of Asia later said that everyone would get a place to stay.
Star cricketers have voiced fears about a lack of top-notch hotels.
A South Korean Olympic committee official told AFP that, with the Games just days away, there are problems.

“At the moment there is a serious shortage of accommodation not only for the entire South Korean delegation to the Asian Games, but for delegations from around the world in the Aichi-Nagoya area,” the official said.
“We are doing everything we can to resolve the issue and ensure there are no such problems.”
Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that all his country’s athletes had been given a room.
But “some officials, like coaches, were moved to different hotels and Airbnb”.
Asian Games organisers did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
The Italian cruise ship Costa Serena is due to arrive in Nagoya on Tuesday.
Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on the vessel.
The rest will be in hotels, including in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events will take place. — AFP
e1aaac28747dea0c: MONTREAL, Sept 14 — Prime Minister Mark Carney calls Canada “the most European of non-European countries,” and while formal EU membership may be tricky, he is pursuing unprecedented closeness with the bloc to reduce dependence on a hostile United States.

Carney heads to Strasbourg, France, this week, where he will become the first head of government to attend the “State of the European Union” address on Wednesday, before delivering his own speech at the European Parliament the following day.
He will also make a stop in Liverpool, where he will hold his first meeting with Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham.
His visit is a “tremendous symbol,” said Tobias Cremer, a European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a March resolution calling for stronger EU-Canada cooperation.
“Canada has many of the resources that Europe is very much short of, whether it’s in terms of energy, whether it’s rare earths (and) raw minerals,” Cremer told AFP.
Canada has been hit hard by US President Donald Trump’s trade war given its close economic integration with its southern neighbour, and is urgently seeking new economic partners.
The EU has also been shaken by Trump’s return to office and, like Canada, is seeking to “diversify and de-risk” its foreign relations, Cremer said.
Future EU member?
Carney has already brought Canada closer to the bloc.
Canada became the first non-EU country to join its defence procurement programme, and the prime minister was involved in Canada joining the pop culture extravaganza Eurovision.
Next month, Carney is hosting an EU-Canada summit in Montreal, where he said discussions will begin on building “a much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership.”

Javier Moreno Sanchez, a Spanish EU lawmaker who heads a parliamentary delegation for relations with Canada, noted that Ottawa and Brussels see eye-to-eye on climate and AI, and a digital trade deal is already in the works.
That pact would build on an existing free trade agreement called CETA, which Sanchez said has unrealised potential as small and medium-sized firms are not yet taking advantage of its benefits.
Speculation about full EU membership for Canada has intensified during Trump’s second term.
“We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” Carney told reporters on Sunday.

“What we are looking and will begin discussions for (is) a unique alliance with the European Union,”he said. “We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths.”
Not ‘realistic’
An April poll showed 57 per cent of Canadians backed EU membership, but it’s not clear whether Canada is even eligible.
Article 49 of the EU treaty states that “a European state” committed to “human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality and the rule of law (and) respect for human rights” can join the bloc.
The treaty does not specify the geographical criteria of a European state, but it’s hard to imagine Canada qualifies.

“The idea of Canada becoming a member of the European Union, either on economic or political terms — I don’t really see that this is a realistic prospect,” said Ignacio Garcia Bercero, an analyst at the Brussels think tank Bruegel.
In 1987, Morocco was denied membership on grounds that it was not a European state.
Sanchez joked that Canada “wasn’t that far” geographically overall, given its proximity to the Danish autonomous territory of Greenland.
But close ties with the EU are possible without full membership, as is the case for Iceland and Switzerland, he said.
Unlike with Switzerland, shipping goods between Canada and the EU comes with substantial transport costs and Europe will never replace the American market for Canada.
In July, 70 per cent of Canadian exports went to the US, compared with just five per cent to the EU.
Still, “the closer we can cooperate, the better,” Cremer said. — AFP
de6079565fd10dd4: BINTULU, Sept 14 — After more than a century of Iban settlement in Sera, Sebauh, Judy Stephen has become the first woman to take on the role of tuai rumah (longhouse chieftain), and she is the 10th to lead this community.
For her, the appointment is a special milestone.
“I feel that No 10 is a good number. I am also very grateful to be the first woman to take over the headship.
“I know it will not be easy, but I am ready to do my best.”
Judy, 60, was officially appointed the tuai rumah on July 1 this year, succeeding her uncle TR Jack Sigie.
Her appointment is significant not only because she is the first woman to lead her community, but also because her longhouse has a history stretching back more than 130 years.
A longhouse with a long history
Judy’s longhouse is located about 50km from Bintulu. It can be reached by both road and river, although the former can sometimes be a challenging journey.
Visitors travelling by car have to park near the Sera River and cross the river to reach the longhouse.
The present longhouse stands on the same general site where Judy’s ancestors settled after moving from Ulu Skrang during the time of the Second Rajah of Sarawak, Sir Charles Brooke.
According to Judy, the first settlement was established sometime in the 1860s, when her great-great-grandfather Bulan Genaya was issued the “Internal Migration Permit” by the Rajah.
From Ulu Skrang, they landed at Nanga Sebauh River, where they built their temporary longhouse.
The original longhouse was a traditional structure, with belian (ironwood) used extensively for the roof, walls and floor.
Even the ruai, the common passage where longhouse residents gather and community life takes place, was made from belian.
Like many established longhouses, Judy’s has been rebuilt several times — the last reconstruction took place in 1989.
For Judy, seeing the longhouse continue to grow is something she looks forward to.
“I have inherited 18 doors, or families. Some families are still working elsewhere. It is exciting to think about how our longhouse can grow in the future,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
(From right) Judy with her daughters, Charraine and Pheonnie, during the Gawai Dayak celebration at the longhouse. — The Borneo Post pic
From Ulu Skrang to Sebauh
The story of the Sera settlement began with the early Iban pioneers who travelled from Ulu Skrang to this Bintulu area during the rule of Rajah Charles Brooke.
Judy’s family history is closely connected with this migration.

Her great-great-grandfather Bulan was among the early Iban migrants from Nanga Bunu in Ulu Skrang. The family history records that he had been involved in the struggles of the time before eventually choosing a more peaceful path.
His son, Jelani Rekan, later became a key figure of the community.
The early Iban settlers arrived in Bintulu, explored the Pandan, Ulu Kemena and Sera areas, where they sourced forest products such as rattan and wild rubber to be traded for cash.
Over time, these temporary camps became permanent settlements.
Judy said the original longhouse was much larger than it is today.
“The original longhouse had 56 bilik (household units). In those days, longhouses were really long,” she recalled.
Over the generations, some families eventually moved away and established new longhouses.
One of the closest breakaway communities is Rumah Tabor, located on the opposite bank of the Sera River.
However, not all of the Sera community joined the breakaway in 2009.
Many families, including Judy’s, continue living in the present longhouse.
For Judy, these movements are part of the natural history of Iban communities.
“It’s the people’s choice, and it cannot be prevented from happening.
“Families sometimes move away because of work, farming opportunities, or because of disputes or disagreements, or simply the desire to establish a new settlement.”
Judy’s uncle Jack was appointed the chieftain in 2009.

His predecessors were Tabor Lasah who led the longhouse from 1979 to 2009; Sigie Ugam (1971-1979); Anggot Manjan (1955-1971); Nilie Rurong (1933-1955); Akat Buja (1932-1933); Jalin Mambang (1913-1932); Bantin Apai Lingang (1896-1913); and Chaong Apai Tayok (1889-1895).
Judy now carries the responsibility of continuing that line of leadership.
Love for books
Judy grew up in a family where education was highly valued.
She is the daughter of Maria Abok and Stephen Randi Sekalai, two of the early educated Ibans from the Sebauh area.
Her father was a Bintulu Town Council officer before becoming involved in private construction.
He was among the early Iban intellectuals who studied at Batu Lintang School and College in Kuching.
Her mother was the daughter of Temenggong Datuk Abok Jalin, a paramount Iban community leader.
Such upbringing encouraged Judy to look beyond the immediate present.
As a young girl, she dreamed of becoming a librarian because she loved books.
The first novel she read was Anne of Green Gables — a 1908 novel by the Canadian author, Lucy Maud Montgomery — which she borrowed from the then-Kuching State Library.
That love has never left her. Today, her home has a sizeable collection of books.
“You can see books everywhere in my home!” she said with a laugh.
Judy was educated at St Teresa’s School in Kuching and later attended Kolej Tun Haji Bujang in Miri for her Form 6 studies.
She furthered her studies in the UK, but was recalled because of the country’s economic downturn.
Nevertheless, she went on to develop a wide range of interests and skills.
She has training in banking, having worked in Bank Utama (the predecessor of today’s RHB Bank) for 10 years, but later resigned due to family commitment.
She is an artisan baker and runs FreyaCraft Bintulu, a business that reflects her interest in sewing and handicrafts.
She hopes to continue her sewing activities after having settled into her new responsibilities as tuai rumah.
Despite her busy schedule, Judy is currently studying law.
For her, learning is clearly a lifelong journey.
Life shaped by responsibility
Judy’s life has also not been without challenges.
She married Sudin Manja of Machan, Kanowit, in 1990, but he passed away in 2009.
She then raised her two daughters, Charraine and Pheonnie — both in their 30s now — on her own.
She and her daughters then relocated to Kuala Lumpur and stayed there for 15 years before returning home to take care of her elderly parents.
Her experience as a mother and widow has given her an understanding of the responsibilities that come with caring for a family.
Today, Judy brings that experience into her role as a community leader.
One of the things Judy is particularly proud of is the primary school located near her longhouse.
SK Hermanus Assan was established in 1963 after the then-Penghulu Abok Jalin appealed to the Sarawak government for a school to serve the children of the surrounding longhouses in Sera.
He then named the school after his brother, Hermanus Assan, the first Iban District Officer in Sarawak.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Judy holds her grandchild Elijah Yusuf, the son of her daughter Charraine and Mohd Yusri Mohd Yarabi. — The Borneo Post pic
Before the school was built, the children had to travel to Central Upper Primary School in Sebauh, which was a difficult journey.
Some even gave up studying altogether.
The first school building was simple — a wooden structure accommodating 30 children from seven nearby longhouses.
Over the years, enrolment grew and today, the school has some 73 pupils.
For the community, the school is more than just a place of learning. It is part of the history of Sera and a reminder of the importance earlier generations placed on education.
Keeping community safe
Today, however, Judy has a grave concern — the crocodile-infested Sera River.
For families whose children have to cross the river by boat, this is a serious matter.
“Our greatest concern is the safety of our children when they cross the river. We have seen crocodiles during the day and at night,” she said.
Teachers and the security guard take precautions when the children travel by boat, but Judy believes the community should not have to live with this worrying concern.
She hopes the government would consider building a bridge across the river.

4f419abe4687ad2a: SEPTEMBER 14 — The latest surge in oil prices is no longer merely an energy story. It is becoming a test of political stability, economic resilience and strategic discipline across Malaysia and Asean.
Brent crude climbed above US$108 (RM438) a barrel on Monday after drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its crucial East-West pipeline.

The pipeline has assumed exceptional importance because it allows Saudi crude to move from the Gulf side of the kingdom to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the increasingly constrained Strait of Hormuz.
The danger is therefore becoming more serious.
West Asia is confronting pressure at several points simultaneously.
The Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted. The Saudi East-West pipeline has been attacked.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have expanded their position around the Bab al-Mandab, including strategic islands commanding approaches to one of the world’s most important maritime passages.

These developments matter profoundly to Asean. In Malaysia alone, the energy subsidies of the federal government used to be RM780 million prior to war on February 28, 2026. It’s now RM 11.3 billion a month.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim can’t help but seethe from the financial implications of his government.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Rising oil prices are putting pressure on Malaysia’s fuel subsidies, transportation costs, business margins and government finances as the West Asia conflict disrupts global energy markets. — Bernama pic
Yet he has retained the subsidies to prevent the Malaysian economy from tail spinning into the bottom.
South-east Asia may be geographically removed from the fighting, but economically it sits well within the blast radius.
The first transmission mechanism is energy.
Oil above US$100 a barrel raises transportation, electricity, aviation, manufacturing and logistics costs.
It eventually feeds into food prices because agriculture, fertilisers, refrigeration and distribution all require energy.
The second transmission mechanism is shipping.
Reuters reports that diverting tankers around Africa can add about 22 days to voyages, while tanker rates have already reached record levels.

For Asean, one of the world’s most trade-dependent regions, this matters enormously. Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines are deeply integrated into global production networks.
Higher shipping and insurance costs eventually appear somewhere in the price of intermediate goods or finished products.
The third transmission mechanism is inflation.
If energy prices remain elevated, central banks face an unpleasant choice.
They can tolerate higher inflation or maintain tighter monetary conditions for longer. Either way, households and businesses feel the consequences.
This is precisely why political stability in Malaysia and Asean must now be treated as an economic asset.
Malaysia has certain advantages. It remains an important oil and gas producer.
Its energy infrastructure, fiscal instruments and relatively diversified economy provide buffers that several other Asean economies do not possess.
But Malaysia cannot regard itself as insulated.
Higher global crude prices affect domestic fuel subsidies, transportation costs, business margins and government finances. They also influence expectations.
Once households and businesses begin anticipating persistent inflation, controlling the secondary effects becomes considerably harder.
The unity government therefore needs policy continuity.
This is not the moment for Malaysia to become consumed by endless political manoeuvring, speculative changes of government or campaigns that undermine confidence in national institutions.
Investors confronting geopolitical uncertainty in West Asia will naturally favour countries that appear predictable.
Political stability consequently acquires a monetary value.
The same principle applies across Asean.
Indonesia needs stability to maintain investor confidence and manage its enormous domestic market.

Thailand requires policy predictability for tourism, manufacturing and exports. Vietnam needs dependable energy supplies to sustain its manufacturing expansion. The Philippines remains particularly exposed to imported fuel costs.
Singapore, despite its formidable financial strength, cannot escape disruptions to shipping, refining and global trade.
Asean therefore faces a common external shock even though its members experience it differently.
This should encourage greater regional coordination rather than economic nationalism.
Asean governments should strengthen energy contingency planning, diversify crude and LNG sourcing, improve strategic stockpiles where appropriate and accelerate regional energy connectivity.
The Asean Power Grid becomes even more important in such an environment.
But infrastructure alone cannot solve the problem.
Governments must retain public confidence.
When oil prices rise sharply, political narratives can deteriorate quickly. Opposition parties attack governments. Governments search for fiscal buffers.
Consumers become angry about living costs. Businesses delay investment. Social media magnifies every increase at the petrol station or supermarket.
The greatest danger is therefore the interaction between external geopolitical shocks and internal political fragmentation.
Asean cannot control what happens in Iran, Saudi Arabia, Iraq or Yemen. Nor can Asean guarantee freedom of navigation through Hormuz or Bab al-Mandab.
What Asean can control is its own resilience.
Indeed, the attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline carries a larger strategic lesson. Diversification itself is vulnerable.
The pipeline was valuable precisely because it provided an alternative to Hormuz. Once that alternative came under attack, the world’s margin for manoeuvre narrowed considerably.
Markets understand this. That is why Brent moved so quickly above US$108. Earlier this year, oil had already reached about US$126 a barrel before retreating.
A return towards those levels cannot be dismissed if the West Asian crisis deteriorates further.
Malaysia and Asean should consequently prepare for a prolonged period of expensive energy rather than assume that every spike will rapidly disappear.
Preparation requires sound fiscal management, diversified energy sources, stronger Asean cooperation and carefully targeted assistance to vulnerable households.
Above all, it requires political stability.
Malaysia cannot stabilise the Strait of Hormuz.
Asean cannot determine the military balance in Yemen. Neither can prevent drones from attacking pipelines thousands of kilometres away.
But Malaysia and Asean can ensure that geopolitical instability abroad does not produce political instability at home.
That may prove to be one of the most important economic defences South-east Asia possesses during the difficult final quarter of 2026.
* Phar Kim Beng is a professor of Asean Studies, and director at the Institute of International and Asean Studies, International Islamic University Malaysia.
** This is the personal opinion of the writers or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
f53b5f7e60ddc3ef: Microsoft has confirmed that its latest security updates can disrupt Remote Desktop Services, silence some USB audio devices, and break pasting in Excel. September's Windows patches hardly support Microsoft's insistence that it is sorting out quality. The known issues list suggests there's still work to do. Reports of problems with Remote Desktop Services (RDS) began circulating on social media shortly after the update, and Microsoft has now acknowledged that, for some users, RDS has indeed been broken across multiple Windows versions, including Windows 11 26H1 and Windows Server 2012. The latter is due to drop out of the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program on October 13, 2026, so perhaps administrators might consider this a going-away present from Microsoft? Connections might fail after a few minutes, servers might hang at "Please wait for the Remote Desktop Configuration," and so on. "Related tools, including Microsoft Management Console (MMC), RDS Licensing Diagnoser, and File Explorer might also become unresponsive," Microsoft admitted. "Additionally, the Windows Update page might stop responding and continuously display a loading indicator." If a virtual machine becomes inaccessible through RDP, stopping (deallocating) and restarting it might temporarily restore connectivity. Microsoft is working on a fix. Microsoft also confirmed issues with support for some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices on Windows 11 26H1, 25H2, and 24H2. The standard dates back to the previous century, but affected users might find themselves with no audio, broken sound settings and volume controls, or problems with multichannel audio. Some customers have restored audio by switching to two-channel mode, Microsoft says. The company is working on a fix but has not provided a timeline. Users of Microsoft's productivity applications were not left out. either A fix for Excel remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities has broken a basic spreadsheet function. "The paste operation might fail silently," according to Microsoft. Excel 2016, 2019, 2021, and 2024 are affected. Microsoft said: "Although users try to paste content, the source remains selected and the destination is unmodified. When this issue occurs, users receive no indication of the failure, such as a beep or error message." The bad news for users with automatic updating turned on is that this update could have already been downloaded and installed automatically. Microsoft has not published a workaround, and one forum user reported resolving the issue by uninstalling and reinstalling Office, while others reported success using commands to uninstall the security update. Removing the update also removes its security fixes. ®
b01ec1a6fc6bdaa0: PETALING JAYA: A residents' group has questioned the proposed reclamation for the Jelutong landfill rehabilitation project from an initial 4ha to 28ha.

Protect Karpal Singh Drive Action Committee (ProtectKarpal) said the area appears to be intended mainly for processing and recycling excavated waste rather than securing the landfill perimeter as required under the project agreement.
The committee said the joint development agreement (JDA) only allowed additional reclamation where it was necessary to secure the perimeter for the rehabilitation works.
It said the displayed environmental impact assessment (EIA) appeared to indicate that almost all of the proposed 28ha would be used for processing and recycling excavated waste.
“A need for waste-processing space does not, by itself, establish a need for perimeter security,” it said in a statement.

ProtectKarpal said Clause 1.1.1 of the JDA defined the “Additional Area” as land the developer rehabilitates beyond the existing area, but only “as required and approved by the relevant authorities to secure the perimeters for the purpose of the developer carrying out and completing the rehabilitation works only”.
This meant that the state government should only approve additional reclamation that could be shown to be necessary for perimeter security, rather than allowing the full 28ha.
The group said PLB Engineering Bhd’s revised tender in July 2016 had proposed no sea reclamation.

It said that when the JDA was signed in February 2020, chief minister Chow Kon Yeow had told the public that “up to 10 acres (4ha) of additional land would be reclaimed for embankment works and parameter wall”.
The figure had since increased to 28ha in the EIA put on public display in February 2025.
“This is seven times what the chief minister described five years earlier,” it said.

ProtectKarpal also warned against using waste recovered from the Jelutong landfill as fill material for the reclamation, saying this could risk creating another landfill along the reclaimed coastline.
It said describing the material as “recycled” did not establish that it was environmentally safe for marine reclamation and called for independent evidence that the fill was suitable.

ProtectKarpal said the state government had an option to terminate the JDA under Clause 18.1, which allows termination with at least 30 days' notice if the state considers it necessary in the state interest, for state security, or for government or public policy.
It said the state should explain publicly if it anticipated compensation or other legal consequences from terminating the agreement.
The RM1 billion project involves rehabilitating the old Jelutong landfill and reclaiming 28.3ha of coastal land beside Karpal Singh Drive.
The landfill, about 3km from George Town’s heritage centre, has been used since the early 1970s, with only construction debris and garden waste allowed there since 2002.
Residents have previously called for the reclamation to be dropped, saying the original plan was to rehabilitate the landfill and provide green space.
The state has said the reclaimed land is needed to sort and recycle waste from the landfill before the site is cleaned up and developed.
b75e6eeb973d53ee: LONDON: Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said he is still learning which players can cope with the demands of playing every three days as his side prepare to host Tottenham Hotspur in the League Cup third round on Tuesday.

940741dcec0ef5f0: Huawei wants near-packaged optics (NPO) standardized for AI networks, pitching it as a replacement for conventional pluggable modules without the cost and maintenance headaches it attributes to co-packaged optics. The Chinese tech giant showcased an NPO module with a capacity of 7.2 terabits per second (Tbps) at the China International Optoelectronic Exposition (CIOE) held in Shenzhen over September 9-11, and said this will form part of the company's next-gen SuperPOD AI systems. NPO refers to the placement of the optical engine in a network switch as close as possible to the switch's application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), but still as a separate package plugged into the mainboard. This is one potential option to supersede the pluggable modules now widely used to terminate optical fiber links to a switch. Pluggable modules typically contain a digital signal processor (DSP) to clean up the incoming signal, and their power consumption and heat output increase with network speed. With AI infrastructure pushing network connections to 800 Gbps and even 1.6 Tbps, this is becoming a problem. Another upgrade path for switches is co-packaged optics (CPO), where the optical engine sits even closer – on the same substrate as the switch ASIC silicon. This is expected to deliver low latency and power consumption, but Huawei says the advanced packaging is expensive and makes failed optical engines difficult to replace in the datacenter. This is why Huawei says it is pushing NPO as the pragmatic choice for the near future. "When it comes to optical interconnects, there are two technical choices. One is NPO, near package optics. The other is CPO, co-packaged optics. Compared with CPO, the NPO technology is more mature, making it easier for production ramp up and it's easier for maintenance. So NPO stands as the most mature technology at the moment, and it is also a practical choice in this day and age," said Dr Man Jiangwei, director of Huawei's Advanced Opto-Electronics Laboratory. Huawei says its NPO design eliminates the module's separate DSP by integrating those functions into the ASIC. Man claims this cuts latency from 100 nanoseconds to 10 nanoseconds and reduces power consumption by around 60 percent. "When you put all these factors together, we're able to bring down the cost by a large margin," he claimed. But a project to define NPO standards was officially started only in May this year, at the Q2 meeting of the Optical Internetworking Forum (OIF). Its members include Cisco, HPE, Arista, and Nvidia. The members there were focused on defining a 6.4 Tbps NPO interface with a future extension to 12.8 Tbps, while Huawei is already demonstrating its 7.2 Tbps product. Asked about this at a roundtable to discuss NPO, Dr Man said 6.4T and 7.2T represent the fan-out bandwidth capabilities required by different vendors and system players. "I believe this kind of technical divergence or differing opinions is quite common in standardization. Looking ahead on the standards platform, I'm confident we'll find an appropriate way to ensure compatibility between 6.4T and 7.2T, meeting the needs of the entire industry chain," he said. One of the goals of the OIF NPO project is to come up with common electrical interfaces, mechanical form factors and connectors. Huawei's NPO is understood to employ 200 gigabits per second per lane across a total of 36 lanes, while the proposed 6.4 Tbps OIF interface would use 32 lanes. The company has already committed to using its own NPO in the upcoming third generation of its SuperPOD AI infrastructure platform, an analog of Nvidia's NVL rack-scale systems. The SuperPOD platform links large numbers of Huawei's Ascend neural processing units (NPUs). Huawei declined to say when this SuperPOD will be available, but Dr Man hinted more will be revealed at the Huawei Connect event in Shanghai later this week. He also said Huawei will be "more than happy to share this product with our customers in the downstream, and not only downstream, but we also like to share this technology with the suppliers on the upstream, including various vendors from different countries and regions." Huawei's exposure to US export restrictions, imposed on national security and foreign policy grounds, raises a related question. One roundtable participant asked whether industry adoption could suffer if the Trump administration perceives NPO as Huawei-driven technology. Man said he wasn't the right person to discuss the political environment and reiterated Huawei's commitment to openness and collaboration. "We are happy to work with vendors from different regions, including vendors from the United States, from China, and from Japan. So together we can advance the development of the NPO ecosystem and ultimately contribute to the booming AI ecosystem," he said. NPO isn't the only alternative to CPO. Earlier this year, Arista Networks unveiled its eXtra-dense Pluggable Optics (XPO) concept, which proposes updating pluggable modules to include cooling via an integrated liquid cooling cold plate, and offering up to 12.8 Tbps per module (64 lanes at 200 Gbps each). Huawei pitches NPO as the most mature option; XPO retains the front-panel plug-in module format. Which format will get the widest adoption will depend on switch vendor support as well as customer priorities, and it is likely that NPO, CPO and XPO will coexist for some time. ®
270c9c594e5208a6: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 14 — Malaysia is in a stronger position than a decade ago, thanks to major fiscal decisions by the government, such as subsidy cuts and a focus on economic development, said Securities Commission Malaysia (SC) chairman Datuk Mohammad Faiz Azmi.
He said the country’s improved financial position was also reflected in the recent pricing of its US dollar Government Sukuk issuance, which demonstrated stronger international recognition.

“Malaysia already offers a deep and diversified capital market which is bigger than banking assets, recognised leadership in Islamic finance, sound regulatory and governance foundations, as well as having a firm commitment to strengthening cross-border connectivity,” he said at the Asean Investment Roadshow today.

Mohammad Faiz said efforts to improve the vibrancy and growth of Malaysia’s capital market were being undertaken under the Capital Market Masterplan 2026-2030 (CMP), including through initiatives such as MY Value Up with Bursa Malaysia involving the country’s top 88 public-listed companies.

The SC had also recently signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission to establish a framework for single-prospectus dual-listed initial public offerings and cross-listing of eligible REITs and ETFs, aimed at widening market access, providing more options for issuers and investors and deepening cross-border participation.
Mohammad Faiz also said Asean regulators had agreed last year on five key initiatives, including pursuing consistent voluntary carbon market standards and implementing the Asean Taxonomy Version 4.

The initiatives also included issuing a simplified environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosure guide for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Asean and developing a project guide to identify pilot projects for blended finance for adaptation and resilience funding.

He said the Asean Capital Markets Forum (ACMF) Action Plan 2026-2030 comprised five strategic thrusts, 11 key priorities and 18 initiatives aimed at strengthening regional integration and Asean’s global positioning.

“Four key initiatives in the ACMF Action Plan related to strengthening regional integration and global positioning are to promote Asean Diamonds, facilitate the creation of Asean indices, create a renewed focus on Islamic Finance, which is a differentiator for our markets, with a better shariah screening tool, and to facilitate intra-Asean activities, products and connectivity,” said Mohammad Faiz.
He said a key priority was to establish a committee to promote Asean as an asset class, currently led by the Philippines and Singapore.

Greater regional connectivity and international participation would be crucial to Asean’s next phase of growth, while calling on investors to reconsider Asean as a strategic long-term investment destination, said Mohammad Faiz. — Bernama
431323fa8d0d3ac9: PANDEGLANG (Indonesia), Sept 14 — Indonesian rescuers on Monday extended the search for eight people, including five journalists, a week after their speedboat went missing in the waters between the islands of Java and Sumatra, an official said.
The Indonesian journalists were on a trip to take photos and videos of the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau, which blanketed cities in volcanic ash and prompted multiple airports to close.

The group, which also included two crew members and a guide, set out by boat from an area west of capital Jakarta on the afternoon of September 7, but lost contact somewhere in the Sunda Strait soon after.

“We will continue the search for the next three days.”

Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in the South-east Asian archipelago, due in part to lax safety standards and inclement weather.
Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity. — AFP

Roundtables: could AI really kill us all?

This geneticist’s age-reversal tech could help restore sight

Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is obsessed with aging. And with eyes. As he steps outside the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, his aviator glasses darken automatically in the sun. Age-related blindness runs in his family, and his own 23andMe test came back with a mutation for macular degeneration, a top cause of vision loss in old age.

That obsession extends to his work. Lu is behind one of the coolest results in rejuvenation science and eye research: an age-reversal technique called reprogramming that repaired the optic nerves of blind mice, restoring their vision. Now, nearly the same genetic therapy he developed as a student has entered human clinical trials.
